analysis.one_liner: Imposes an excise tax on large corporations whose CEOs earn more than 50 times their median worker's pay.
analysis.headline: The bill never received a hearing or vote: it was referred to the Senate Finance Committee on the day it was introduced and stayed there until the 118th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would charge large companies a tax if their highest-paid executive earns more than 50 times the wages of their median worker. It applies only to companies with at least $100 million in annual receipts and $10 million in payroll, and the tax is capped at 1% of a company's gross receipts. The idea is to give companies a financial reason to narrow the gap between executive pay and everyone else's pay.
analysis.who_benefits: If it passed, workers at large companies where executives are paid vastly more would gain the most. The tax is designed to pressure employers to either raise typical wages or moderate executive pay, and revenue would flow to the Treasury. It also builds on a disclosure rule that already requires public companies to report their CEO-to-worker pay ratio, but unlike disclosure, this puts a price on the gap itself.

how_it_helps.text: The bill imposes an excise tax on employers whose CEO-to-median-worker pay ratio exceeds 50 to 1, with the tax growing as the gap widens beyond that threshold.
It applies to companies with at least $100 million in annual gross receipts and $10 million in payroll, measured over three years, so small businesses are not touched.

The tax counts bonuses, stock awards, and options as executive pay, so compensation cannot be hidden by paying executives mainly in stock, and it includes rules allowing regulators to prevent companies from lowering the measured ratio by replacing employees with contractors.
The tax is capped at 1% of a company's gross receipts, limiting the maximum burden on any single firm.

analysis.who_pays: Large corporations with extreme executive pay would pay the tax, and top executives at those firms would face pressure on their compensation. Some of the tax's cost could ultimately be passed to shareholders through lower profits or to consumers through prices; companies might also choose to raise low-end wages, which is part of the intended effect.
analysis.who_pays_short: Large corporations with big pay gaps

drawbacks.text: The tax is levied on the company, not the executive, so a firm can simply pay the tax and leave executive pay and worker pay unchanged; shareholders or consumers, not the CEO, may absorb the cost.
The tax is capped at 1% of gross receipts, so for a very large, high-revenue company even an extreme pay gap would trigger a comparatively modest charge.

Measuring the pay ratio is complex: the bill averages the executive's pay over five years against the median for a single year, and firms could restructure their workforces or use contractors, which the bill only addresses through future Treasury regulations rather than statutory rules.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill targets a real and widely cited phenomenon — very large gaps between executive pay and typical worker pay — and applies only to very large companies, so small businesses are spared. But its design is soft: the tax is capped, it is paid by the company rather than the executive, and firms can avoid changing behavior by simply paying it. As a nudge toward narrowing pay gaps it is modest; as a revenue measure it is small.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced and immediately referred to the Senate Finance Committee, which never scheduled a hearing, markup, or vote, and it died there when the 118th Congress ended.

narrative.text: Sheldon Whitehouse introduced the bill in the Senate on November 1, 2023, with Elizabeth Warren and Jeff Merkley joining as cosponsors — three senators in total.
The same day, the bill was read twice and referred to the Senate Finance Committee.
No further action appears in the record: no hearing, no markup, no committee vote, and no floor vote ever occurred before the Congress ended on January 3, 2025.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Large corporations with extreme executive-to-worker pay gaps are better off, because the excise tax was never seriously advanced and never became law, so no company will pay it. Their shareholders and executives keep the current compensation structure unchanged.

for.name: Sheldon Whitehouse
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and assigned it to the Senate Finance Committee.

against.name: Senate Finance Committee
against.role: Committee of jurisdiction over tax legislation
against.what_they_did: Received the referral on November 1, 2023 and took no recorded action — no hearing, markup, or vote — for the rest of the Congress.

against.name: Ron Wyden
against.what_they_did: As chair of the committee holding the bill, never scheduled it for a hearing or markup.

against.name: 49 of 49 Senate Republicans
against.what_they_did: No Republican signed on as a cosponsor, leaving the bill without the bipartisan backing typically needed to move tax legislation.

sides.party_line_note: All three supporters were Democrats (3 of 48 Senate Democrats cosponsored) and no Republican cosponsored, so the bill never had a cross-party base to build a vote from.

industries.industry: Large corporations with extreme executive pay (roughly $100M+ in receipts)
industries.note: The bill would tax firms whose CEO earns over 50 times the median worker's pay, though the cap at 1% of gross receipts limits the hit. Its real bite is the pressure it puts on either raising typical wages or trimming executive compensation.

industries.industry: Top executives and executive compensation consultants
industries.note: The tax counts stock awards and options as pay and denies companies a deduction for the excise tax, creating direct pressure to hold down executive compensation packages.

industries.industry: Tax preparation and corporate compliance services
industries.note: A new excise tax with a pay-ratio calculation, aggregation rules, and joint liability would create ongoing compliance and advisory work for large employers.
